_meta.descricao: Catechesis themes on the sacrament of Confirmation, anchored in the Catechism.
_meta.aviso: This is not a complete catechetical itinerary, nor one approved by ecclesiastical authority: each diocese and parish follows its own program of preparation for Confirmation.
_meta.revisao_editorial: All content refers to paragraphs of the Catechism of the Catholic Church and to biblical passages cited by name, without adding any interpretations of its own.

itens.titulo: The Sacrament of Confirmation
itens.resumo: What Confirmation is: a sacrament of Christian initiation that confers the gift of the Holy Spirit and imprints an indelible character.
itens.corpo:
Confirmation is, with Baptism and the Eucharist, one of the three sacraments of Christian initiation. The Catechism teaches that it is necessary for the completion of baptismal grace: the confirmed are enriched with a special strength of the Holy Spirit and more perfectly bound to the Church, so that they may bear witness to Christ.

The origin of the sacrament lies in the laying on of hands by the Apostles. After Pentecost, Peter and John were sent to Samaria to lay hands on the baptized, who thus received the Holy Spirit (Acts 8:14-17), and Paul did the same in Ephesus (Acts 19:6). The CCC (no. 1288) calls the laying on of hands the "origin of the sacrament of Confirmation, which in a certain way perpetuates the grace of Pentecost in the Church." Very early on, to better signify the gift of the Spirit, an anointing with perfumed oil, chrism, was added to the laying on of hands. The term refers to Christ, "whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit" (Acts 10:38). This is why the sacrament is called, in the East, chrismation or myron.

For historical reasons, the original unity between Baptism and Confirmation was broken in the West. As infant baptisms and rural parishes multiplied, it became impossible for the bishop to be present at every celebration. Wishing to reserve the completion of Baptism to the bishop, the West separated the two sacraments in time (CCC 1290); the East kept them united, so that Confirmation is given by the very priest who baptizes, but only with the myron consecrated by a bishop (CCC 1291). It was this separation that gave rise to the current Roman rite, in which, when Confirmation is celebrated separately from Baptism, the liturgy begins with the renewal of the baptismal promises (CCC 1298).

From the ritual standpoint, Western texts only clearly fixed the form of Confirmation in the 12th and 13th centuries. The Roman Pontifical of the 12th century contains for the first time the formula that later became universal: "I sign you with the sign of the cross and confirm you with the chrism of salvation. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." Several ecumenical councils entered the debate on the matter and form: the Profession of Faith of Emperor Michael Palaeologus, read at the Second Council of Lyons, refers to Confirmation conferred by bishops through the laying on of hands when anointing with chrism; the Decree for the Armenians of the Council of Florence defines that the matter of the sacrament is chrism made of oil and balsam, and recalls that "in place of that laying on of the hand, Confirmation is given in the Church"; and the Council of Trent, without defining the essential rite, designated it as the "sacred Chrism of Confirmation." The consecration of the chrism, moreover, in a certain way forms part of the sacrament itself: it is the bishop who consecrates it at the Chrism Mass, on the morning of Holy Thursday, for his whole diocese (CCC 1297).

The essential rite, in the Latin rite, was reaffirmed by Paul VI in the Apostolic Constitution Divinae consortium naturae (August 15, 1971): "The sacrament of Confirmation is conferred through the anointing with holy chrism on the forehead, which is done by the laying on of the hand, and through the words: Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit." The laying on of hands upon the candidates, which precedes the anointing, although it does not belong to the essence of the sacrament, is held in great esteem as it ensures the integrity of the rite. The original minister is the Bishop, successor of the Apostles and possessor of the fullness of the sacrament of Holy Orders; for this reason, his administration of Confirmation highlights the bond of the confirmed with the Church and her apostolic origin. In certain cases and according to the norms of the Church, the priest may confer it. Like Baptism and Holy Orders, Confirmation imprints on the soul an indelible spiritual character and, therefore, is received only once.

itens.titulo: The Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit
itens.resumo: Wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord: the gifts that complete and perfect the virtues, enumerated on the basis of Isaiah 11.
itens.corpo:
The tradition of the Church enumerates seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord. The enumeration is based on the prophecy of Isaiah 11:1-2, a description of the shoot of Jesse upon whom the Spirit of the Lord rests. The number seven does not derive from the original Hebrew text: the Masoretic Text lists six characteristics (wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, and fear of the Lord), with the fear of the Lord mentioned twice. The Greek translation of the Septuagint rendered the first occurrence of fear (the Hebrew root yir'at) also as piety (εὐσεβείας), and the Vulgate of Saint Jerome, which fixed the verse, relied on it: «Spiritus sapientiae et intellectus, spiritus consilii et fortitudinis, spiritus scientiae et pietatis, et replebit eum spiritus timoris Domini» (Is 11:2-3). Saint Ambrose and Saint Augustine saw in the number seven the sign of fullness, and not of an arithmetical count: all desirable gifts dwell in the Messiah.

It was Saint Thomas Aquinas who gave the list its definitive scholastic form, in the treatise on the gifts in the First Part of the Second Part of the Summa Theologica (I-II, q. 68). There he distinguishes the gifts from the virtues — the gifts are habits by which man becomes docile to the impulse of the Holy Spirit, beyond what reason alone would attain — and maintains, in article 4, that they are fittingly enumerated as seven, and, in article 7, that their dignity is grounded in the enumeration of Isaiah 11. Thus the gifts were associated with the virtues and the beatitudes (wisdom with the peacemakers, understanding with those who mourn, counsel with the merciful, fortitude with those who hunger for righteousness, knowledge with those who suffer persecution, piety with the meek, fear with the poor in spirit).

The Catechism of the Catholic Church gathers up this tradition in nos. 1830-1831: the gifts «complete and perfect the virtues of those who receive them» and «make the faithful docile in readily obeying divine inspirations». In this regard it cites Psalm 143 («Let your good spirit lead me on level ground») and the Letter to the Romans («All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God... heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ», Rom 8:14, 17). The Catechism also recalls that the gifts «belong in their fullness to Christ, Son of David» — that is, they belong first to the Messiah and, by participation, to the baptized.

They are not, therefore, extraordinary powers or natural talents, but stable dispositions infused with sanctifying grace, deepened in Baptism and especially strengthened in Confirmation. In Confirmation catechesis, the gifts are presented together with the life of prayer and the sacraments, the ordinary means by which grace is nourished.

itens.titulo: The Fruits of the Holy Spirit
itens.resumo: The twelve fruits that tradition enumerates from Galatians 5:22-23 according to the Vulgate, as signs of the Spirit's action in the Christian life.
itens.corpo:
The fruits of the Holy Spirit are, according to the Catechism (no. 1832), "perfections that the Holy Spirit forms in us as the first fruits of eternal glory." The tradition of the Church lists twelve: charity, joy, peace, patience, forbearance, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faithfulness, modesty, self-control, and chastity — a list that the CCC presents as that of Gal 5:22-23 "according to the Vulgate."

The difference in number with respect to the Greek text is notable and tends to go unnoticed. In the Letter to the Galatians, Saint Paul contrasts the "works of the flesh" (fornication, impurity, idolatry, enmities, jealousy, anger, dissensions, envy, drunkenness, and the like) with the "fruit of the Spirit." The Greek text lists nine: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. The Vulgate of Saint Jerome, in translating, split some of the terms, arriving at the twelve that the Latin tradition consecrated. This is why biblical scholars and denominations that follow the Greek text count nine fruits, while the Catholic catechism and numerous traditional catechisms (the Baltimore Catechism, for example) keep the twelve.

Saint Thomas Aquinas devoted Question 70 of the First Part of the Second Part of the Summa Theologiae to the fruits. He explains that "fruit" has two senses: that which a human being produces and that which he enjoys, that is, the term designates at once the good work and the joy that follows from it. He compares the fruits to the beatitudes: the latter point to the perfection of the saints, while the fruits are more everyday and accessible to those who, even amid struggles, let themselves be led by grace. He organizes them pedagogically according to their order toward one's neighbor and toward oneself.

While the gifts dispose a person to the action of the Spirit, the fruits are the visible effect of that action in conduct: they are the concrete criterion for verifying whether the Christian life is growing. For this reason, preparation for Confirmation does not end on the day of the celebration: it leads into sacramental life, prayer, and charity put into practice, where these fruits ripen.

itens.titulo: The Most Holy Trinity
itens.resumo: One God in three distinct Persons — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — the central mystery of the faith and of Christian life.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism teaches, in numbers 232 to 260, that the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity is "the central mystery of Christian faith and life": only God can make himself known to us by revealing himself as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and this revelation reached its fullness with the sending of the Son and of the Holy Spirit after the Resurrection.

The Church professes one God in three Persons who are truly distinct from one another, yet each wholly God: they are not three gods, nor three modes of a single God who appears now as Father, now as Son, now as Spirit. The divine Persons are distinct by the relations that give them origin — the Father begets the Son, the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son — each remaining equally eternal and almighty.

For this reason every Christian is baptized "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Mt 28:19), and Confirmation, which deepens baptismal grace, is lived as a new gift of this same Trinitarian God, whom in Confirmation catechesis one learns to invoke and to adore as the source of all the life of the Church.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 232-260

itens.titulo: God the Father Almighty, Creator of Heaven and Earth
itens.resumo: The first article of the Creed: God is almighty and Father, and freely created everything that exists, out of nothing and out of love.
itens.corpo:
The Creed opens with the confession "I believe in God, the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth." The Catechism explains, in numbers 268 to 278, that God's omnipotence is not arbitrary: it is manifested above all in the creation of the world and of man, and even more in the Incarnation and Resurrection of his Son, and in his mercy toward sinners.

To create means, for God, to give existence to something that did not exist before, "out of nothing" (ex nihilo), by pure freedom and love, without necessity or effort. This is what number 279 and following teach: the world is not the fruit of chance nor a necessary emanation of God, but a free gift that continues to depend on him at every moment.

Among all visible creatures, the human being is created "in the image and likeness of God" (Gen 1:26-27), capable of knowing and loving his Creator, called to care for creation and to live in communion with him — a truth that Confirmation catechesis takes up again as the foundation of all the faith that is professed.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 268-278, 279-324

itens.titulo: Divine Revelation
itens.resumo: How God progressively makes himself known to human beings, in a dialogue that reaches its fullness in Jesus Christ.
itens.corpo:
God, out of pure goodness, chose to reveal himself and to communicate himself to human beings, inviting them to enter into communion with him. The Catechism, in numbers 50 to 73, describes this revelation as a journey: God made himself known to the patriarchs, spoke through the prophets, and finally, "in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son" (Heb 1:1-2).

The revelation in Jesus Christ is definitive and complete: in him, God said everything he had to say about himself, even though it falls to the Church, over the centuries, to penetrate ever more deeply its meaning. For this reason, there will be no new public revelation before the glorious coming of Christ.

This revelation is transmitted to the Church in two complementary ways — Sacred Scripture and living Tradition — both entrusted to the Magisterium to be interpreted faithfully and taught to each generation, which gives Confirmation catechesis its ultimate foundation: it is not a human opinion, but something that comes from God.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 50-73
Second Vatican Council, Dogmatic Constitution Dei Verbum, no. 2

itens.titulo: Sacred Scripture
itens.resumo: The Bible as the Word of God put into writing, inspired by the Holy Spirit and read in the living faith of the Church.
itens.corpo:
Sacred Scripture brings together the books of the Old and New Testaments, recognized by the Church as inspired by God: they have God as their author, even though they were written by true human authors, who used their own faculties and powers. The Catechism treats this subject in numbers 101 to 141.

The two Testaments form a unity, for "the New Testament lies hidden in the Old and the Old Testament is made manifest in the New," according to the classic formula cited by the Catechism itself. All of Scripture converges on Christ and is fully understood only in Him.

The Church does not read the Bible in isolation: she interprets it in the light of the same Tradition and under the watchful care of the Magisterium, attentive to the content and unity of the whole of Scripture, to the living Tradition, and to the analogy of faith. For this reason, Confirmation catechesis invites the confirmand to become familiar with the prayerful reading of the Word of God, and not only with its doctrine.

itens.titulo: Jesus Christ, Only Son of God
itens.resumo: Second article of the Creed: the confession that Jesus is the Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, the Lord.
itens.corpo:
The second article of the Creed professes: "I believe in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord." The Catechism, in numbers 422 to 451, explains the meaning of each of these names: "Jesus" means "God saves"; "Christ" translates "Messiah," the Anointed One awaited by Israel; "Son of God" affirms the unique and eternal relationship of Jesus with the Father; "Lord" acknowledges in him divine sovereignty.

Faith in Jesus as the Son of God is not one opinion among others: it is the center of the Christian faith, confessed by Peter at Caesarea Philippi — "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God" (Mt 16:16) — and reaffirmed by the Church in every age as the touchstone of true faith.

To recognize Jesus as the only Son of God also implies welcoming his mission: He came to reveal the Father and to reconcile humanity with God, giving his life as a ransom for all. This is the heart of what Confirmation catechesis seeks to deepen in the life of each confirmand.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 422-451

itens.titulo: The Incarnation of the Word
itens.resumo: The Son of God became man, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, remaining God and assuming a true human nature.
itens.corpo:
The third article of the Creed professes that Jesus Christ "was conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary." The Catechism, in numbers 456 to 483, asks about the reason for this Incarnation: the Word became flesh to save us by reconciling us with God, so that we might know God's love, to be a model of holiness, and to make us "partakers of the divine nature" (cf. 2 Pet 1:4).

The faith of the Church professes that, in the Incarnation, the Son of God did not cease to be God by assuming human nature: he is truly God and truly man, united in one divine Person, without confusion or separation between the two natures — a truth solemnly defined by the Council of Chalcedon.

The virginal motherhood of Mary, who conceived by the work of the Holy Spirit, is a sign that this generation is entirely a divine work: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you [...] therefore the child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God" (Lk 1:35), the words of the angel that Confirmation catechesis takes up in order to deepen the mystery of the Christian Christmas.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 456-483

itens.titulo: The Passion and Death of Jesus
itens.resumo: The suffering, crucifixion, and death of Christ under Pontius Pilate: the sacrifice that reconciles humanity with God.
itens.corpo:
The fourth article of the Creed confesses that Jesus Christ "suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried." The Catechism, in numbers 571 to 630, situates this event in concrete history, under an identifiable Roman governor, and at the same time within God's eternal plan of salvation.

The death of Jesus on the cross was not a tragic accident but, according to the faith of the Church, a gift freely offered out of love: "Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures" (1 Cor 15:3). In it, Christ offered himself to the Father as the perfect sacrifice, making reparation for human disobedience by his obedience of love to the end.

The Catechism insists that this death has the value of universal redemption: Christ died for all, without exception, and his Passion continues to be made present in every Eucharist celebrated by the Church, a central theme taken up in Confirmation catechesis as it prepares the confirmand for a Christian life marked by the cross and by charity.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 571-630
John 19

itens.titulo: The Resurrection of Christ
itens.resumo: On the third day Christ rose from the dead: the central event that founds Christian faith and hope.
itens.corpo:
The fifth article of the Creed professes that Jesus "rose again from the dead on the third day." The Catechism, in numbers 631 to 658, calls the Resurrection the "crowning truth" of our faith in Christ, attested as a historical fact by the testimony of the apostles, who saw the Risen One and ate and drank with Him, and handed down as the core of apostolic preaching from the very beginning: "if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile" (cf. 1 Cor 15:14).

The Resurrection is not Jesus' return to ordinary earthly life, but the definitive passage of his humanity, already glorified, into the power of God: for this reason the risen body of Christ is the same one that suffered on the cross, but transformed, free from the limitations of space and time.

For the Christian, the Resurrection of Christ is the pledge and cause of one's own resurrection: "For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive" (1 Cor 15:22), a truth that Confirmation catechesis proposes as the foundation of the hope that sustains the moral and sacramental life of the confirmand.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 631-658

itens.titulo: The Ascension and the Coming of Christ in Glory
itens.resumo: Christ ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father; he will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead.
itens.corpo:
The sixth and seventh articles of the Creed profess that Jesus "ascended into heaven, and is seated at the right hand of the Father, and he will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead." The Catechism treats these two mysteries in numbers 659 to 682.

The Ascension marks the definitive entry of Christ's humanity into the glory of God, forty days after Easter (cf. Acts 1:3, 9-11): Christ did not cease to be present among his own, but his presence now becomes that of the Head who continually intercedes for the Church before the Father.

Christian faith still awaits the glorious coming of Christ at the end of time, when he will judge the living and the dead, revealing the ultimate truth of every conscience and of all history. No one knows the day or the hour of this coming, and for this reason the Church lives in hopeful vigilance, a theme that Confirmation catechesis takes up when speaking of life in the state of grace.

itens.titulo: I Believe in the Holy Spirit
itens.resumo: The eighth article of the Creed: the Holy Spirit, the third Person of the Most Holy Trinity, "the Lord, the giver of life."
itens.corpo:
The eighth article of the Creed professes: "I believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the giver of life." The Catechism, in numbers 683 to 747, teaches that no one can know God as Father, nor confess that Jesus is Lord, except under the action of the Holy Spirit, who already acts in the Old Testament through the prophets and is fully manifested in Christ.

The Holy Spirit is sent by the Father and the Son in a definitive way at Pentecost: "And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit" (Acts 2:4), an event that marks the visible birth of the Church and the beginning of her mission to proclaim the Gospel to all peoples.

Since then, the Holy Spirit continues to act in the Church and in each Christian: in the Scripture he inspired, in the Tradition he guards, in the Magisterium he assists, in the liturgy and the sacraments, and in the prayer of each believer. Confirmation is precisely the sacrament in which this same Spirit is given in a special way, uniting the confirmand more closely to the mission of the Church.

itens.titulo: The Church, Body of Christ and People of God
itens.resumo: Two central biblical images for understanding the nature of the Church: a community called together by God and a living organism united to Christ.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in nos. 781 to 796, presents the Church through several complementary biblical images. As the "People of God," the Church is made up of all those who, through faith and Baptism, have been called to be part of a new covenant, overcoming boundaries of race, nation, or culture: "Once you were no people but now you are God's people" (cf. 1 Pet 2:9-10).

As the "Body of Christ," the Church is a vital communion with Christ, her Head: just as the human body has many members with different functions, so Christians, united to Christ through Baptism, form one body, with a diversity of gifts and ministries at the service of the common good (cf. 1 Cor 12:27).

These two images complement each other: they reveal that the Church is not a mere human organization, but a mystery of communion between God and men, founded on Christ and animated by the Holy Spirit — a truth that Confirmation catechesis takes up again in order to situate the confirmand within this living community.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 781-796

itens.titulo: The Church, Temple of the Holy Spirit
itens.resumo: The Church as the dwelling place of God among men, animated, sanctified, and guided by the Holy Spirit.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in numbers 797 to 801, teaches that "what builds up the Church and makes her live is the Holy Spirit." The Spirit dwells in the faithful as in a temple, unites them with one another and with Christ, and distributes to each one gifts and charisms for the common good of the community.

Saint Paul asks the Christians of Corinth: "Do you not know that you are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in you?" (1 Cor 3:16). The image of the temple indicates that the Church is not merely a visible institution, but a living space where God becomes present and is worshiped "in spirit and truth."

The charisms that the Spirit distributes, whether extraordinary or simple and humble, are not for personal benefit, but for the building up of the Church and her mission in the world, always discerned and ordered by the pastors. This teaching prepares the confirmand to understand the gifts of the Spirit received in Confirmation as service to the community, not as an individual privilege.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 797-801

itens.titulo: The Church Is One
itens.resumo: The first of the four marks of the Church: unity of faith, of sacraments and of governance, lived out in the legitimate diversity of peoples and cultures.
itens.corpo:
The Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed professes the Church as "one, holy, catholic and apostolic." The Catechism treats unity in numbers 813 to 822: the Church is one because she has her source in the unity of the Holy Trinity, was founded by Christ, her only Lord, and is animated by one Spirit.

This unity is manifested concretely in the profession of one faith received from the apostles, in the common celebration of the sacraments, above all the Eucharist, and in apostolic succession through the sacrament of Holy Orders, which maintains communion among all the particular Churches and the successor of Peter.

At the same time, the Catechism recognizes that, throughout history, divisions have arisen among Christians, and for this reason the Catholic Church prays and works for the full unity of all the baptized, in a movement called ecumenism, a theme that Jesus himself asked of the Father on the eve of his death: "that they may all be one" (Jn 17:21).

itens.titulo: The Church Is Holy
itens.resumo: The Church is holy because Christ, her founder, is holy, even though her members remain sinners on the path of conversion.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in numbers 823 to 829, teaches that the Church is "indefectibly holy" because she is united to Christ, her Bridegroom, who gave himself up for her "to make her holy" (Eph 5:25-26), and because the Holy Spirit gives her the life of God. Holiness is, therefore, not an achievement of her members, but a gift that comes from union with Christ. The Second Vatican Council takes up exactly this teaching in chapter V of the constitution Lumen Gentium ("The Universal Call to Holiness in the Church"), when it states: "The faith of the Church teaches that the Church... is indefectibly holy. Indeed, Christ, the Son of God... loved the Church as His bride, delivering Himself up for her so as to sanctify her, and joined her to Himself as His body."

At the same time, the Church recognizes the presence of sin in her midst: therefore she is "at once holy and always in need of purification", following constantly the path of penance and renewal (CCC 827). Number 827 cites Saint Augustine, who compared the Church to a net that gathers good and bad fish, and to the threshing floor that separates the wheat from the chaff: sin exists in her members, but it does not cancel the holiness of Christ who sustains her. A historical clarification that is often wrongly repeated is worth making: the expression "casta meretrix" (literally "chaste harlot") is an oxymoron coined by Saint Ambrose in his Commentary on the Gospel of Saint Luke, applied to the figure of Rahab, and not a common designation used by the Fathers for the Church. It is, in fact, a hapax of patristic literature, and not the usual formula with which the tradition speaks of the Church.

The same number 827 articulates the tension precisely: "While Christ, holy, innocent, undefiled, knew nothing of sin, but came only to expiate the sins of the people, the Church, containing sinners in her own bosom, is at once holy and always in need of being purified." For this reason theologians speak of the Ecclesia semper reformanda — the Church that, holy in Christ, ceaselessly converts in her members.

The holiness of the Church shines forth eminently in Mary and the saints. Number 829 affirms that "in the Most Blessed Virgin, the Church has already reached the perfection whereby she exists without spot or wrinkle", while the other faithful "still strive to increase in holiness": in Mary, the Church is already fully holy. The saints, for their part, show that the grace of Christ truly transforms concrete human lives. This is why Confirmation catechesis presents the lives of the saints as a witness that holiness is not an unattainable ideal, but a path open to every baptized person — a theme the Council formulated when recalling that "all in the Church, whether they belong to the hierarchy or are cared for by it, are called to holiness" (Lumen Gentium, 39).

itens.titulo: The Church Is Catholic
itens.resumo: The universality of the Church, sent by Christ to all peoples with the fullness of the means of salvation.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in numbers 830 to 856, explains that the word "catholic" means "universal," "according to the totality," or "in keeping with the whole." The Church is catholic in two senses: she possesses the fullness of the means of salvation — the complete faith, the sacraments, and the ordained ministry in apostolic succession — and she is sent by Christ to the whole human race, without distinction of people, culture, or era.

Each particular Church, united with its bishop and in communion with the successor of Peter, is truly Church, and in it the one, holy, catholic, and apostolic Catholic Church truly subsists: catholicity does not cancel out the legitimate diversity of traditions and rites, but harmonizes them in one and the same communion.

By her very nature the Church is missionary, sent by Christ with the mandate "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations" (Mt 28:19), a truth taken up again in numbers 849 to 856, which gives Confirmation catechesis the concrete horizon toward which the confirmand is sent.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 830-856

itens.titulo: The Church Is Apostolic
itens.resumo: The Church is built on the foundation of the apostles and remains faithful to their teaching through apostolic succession.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in nos. 857 to 865, teaches that the Church is apostolic in three senses: she was built on the foundation of the apostles, chosen witnesses sent on mission by Christ (cf. Eph 2:20); she guards and transmits, with the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in her, the teaching received from the apostles; and she continues to be taught, sanctified, and governed by the apostles until Christ's return, through their successors, the bishops, in communion with the successor of Peter.

This continuity is not only one of doctrine, but of living mission: each bishop, upon being ordained, receives the same mission that Christ entrusted to the apostles, and through him this mission reaches every diocese and parish.

The original minister of Confirmation is precisely the Bishop, a visible sign of this bond between the person being confirmed and the apostolic Church: when he is confirmed by the Bishop, or in his name, the young person is more closely incorporated into the same mission that goes back to the apostles.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 857-865
Eph 2:20

itens.titulo: Mary, Mother of the Church
itens.resumo: Mary's unique role in the work of salvation, her spiritual motherhood over all the disciples of Christ, and the title proclaimed by Paul VI in 1964.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in numbers 963 to 975, teaches that Mary's motherhood in relation to the Church is an extension of her divine motherhood. The Dogmatic Constitution Lumen Gentium of the Second Vatican Council develops this doctrine in its chapter VIII: Mary, "predestined from eternity to be the Mother of God", cooperated "in an utterly singular way by her obedience, faith, hope and burning charity in the Savior's work" and is, "for this reason, a mother to us in the order of grace" (LG 61). The Council here takes up an argument already formulated by Saint Ambrose and Saint Augustine: if Mary is the Mother of Christ, head of the Church, she cannot fail to be the mother of the members of that body as well (LG 53).

The historical root of the title goes back to the fourth century: Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan (died 397), called the Church mother, virgin and fruitful, and applied the same mystery to Mary — "the Mother of God is the type of the Church in the order of faith, charity and perfect union with Christ, as Saint Ambrose already taught" (LG 63, citing Epistulae 63). In dogmatic definition, the landmark is the Council of Ephesus, the third ecumenical council, held in 431 and convoked by Emperor Theodosius II, which proclaimed Mary Theotókos, "Mother of God", against the position of Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople, who preferred Christotókos ("Mother of Christ"); Saint Cyril of Alexandria presided over the proceedings, with about 250 bishops, between June and July of that year.

From the height of the cross, Jesus entrusted the beloved disciple to Mary and Mary to the disciple — "Behold, your mother" (Jn 19:27) —, a gesture that the Church has always understood as the gift of Mary to every Christian as spiritual mother. Lumen Gentium adds that this motherhood in the economy of grace "will last without interruption until the eternal fulfillment of all the elect", from "the consent which she loyally gave at the Annunciation and which she sustained without wavering beneath the cross": taken up to heaven, Mary "did not lay aside this saving office, but by her manifold intercession continues to bring us the gifts of eternal salvation" (LG 62). This is why the Virgin is invoked as Advocate, Helper, Benefactress and Mediatrix — titles that, the Council stresses, neither take away from nor add anything to the unique and effective mediation of Christ, but depend entirely on it.

The solemn recognition of the title is recent: on November 21, 1964, in the closing address of the third session of the Second Vatican Council, in Saint Peter's Basilica, Pope Paul VI proclaimed Mary "Mother of the Church, that is, of all the People of God, both the faithful and the pastors, who call her the most loving Mother". The proclamation took place against the opinion of some of the German bishops and of the doctrinal commission, concerned about ecumenical appropriateness, but it was received with strong applause from the Council Fathers. In 1980, John Paul II inserted the invocation "Mother of the Church" into the Litany of Loreto.

Later, by decree of the Congregation for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments — the decree Ecclesia Mater, internally dated February 11, 2018 (the anniversary of the first apparition of Our Lady at Lourdes) and published on March 3, 2018 —, Pope Francis inscribed the obligatory memorial of the "Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of the Church" in the General Roman Calendar, to be celebrated on the Monday after Pentecost. Cardinal Robert Sarah, then prefect of the dicastery, summed up the meaning of the feast in the formula "Crux, Hostia et Virgo" — the Cross, the Host and the Virgin —, the three mysteries in which the Christian interior life must be rooted. The Church's devotion to Mary does not replace or diminish the unique mediation of Christ, but manifests it: for this reason, Confirmation catechesis reminds the confirmand that honoring Mary as mother is an inseparable part of maturing in faith in her Son.

itens.titulo: The Communion of Saints
itens.resumo: The spiritual union that binds the faithful still on pilgrimage on earth, the souls being purified, and the saints who already behold God.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in nos. 946 to 962, explains that the expression "communion of saints" has two complementary meanings: communion in "holy things" (sancta), above all faith, the sacraments, and the charisms shared by all the baptized, and communion among "holy persons" (sancti), that is, among all who are united to Christ.

This communion unites three states of the one and the same Church: the faithful still on pilgrimage on earth, those who are being purified after death (the Church suffering, or Purgatory), and the blessed who already behold God face to face (the heavenly Church, the saints). Among these three states there is a real exchange of spiritual goods, above all through prayer and mutual intercession.

This truth underlies central practices of Christian life: the intercession of the saints, prayer for the dead, and the certainty that no Christian walks alone: "surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses" (Heb 12:1), as the Letter to the Hebrews reminds us.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 946-962
Heb 12:1

itens.titulo: The Resurrection of the Body and Life Everlasting
itens.resumo: The final articles of the Creed: the hope of rising again with our own body, glorified, and of living forever in communion with God.
itens.corpo:
The Creed ends with the confession "I believe in the resurrection of the body, and life everlasting." The Catechism treats the resurrection of the body in nos. 988 to 1004: every human being will rise on the last day with the same body he had in life, but transformed and incorruptible, like the glorious body of the risen Christ.

In nos. 1020 to 1060, the Catechism treats eternal life: immediately after death, each soul receives from God its eternal retribution, according to its works and its faith — either entering into full communion with God (heaven), or undergoing a purification necessary before that communion (purgatory), or being definitively separated from God, freely chosen through sin (hell).

At the end of time, with the resurrection of the body and the Last Judgment, this retribution will also reach the body, and God will renew all creation: "Behold, I make all things new" (Rev 21:5). Jesus sums up this hope by saying: "I am the resurrection and the life" (Jn 11:25), words central to Confirmation catechesis on the last things.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 988-1004, 1020-1060
1 Cor 15

itens.titulo: The Seven Sacraments of the Church
itens.resumo: Efficacious signs of grace, instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church, grouped into sacraments of initiation, sacraments of healing, and sacraments at the service of communion.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in nos. 1113 to 1134, defines the sacraments as efficacious signs of grace, instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church, by which divine life is dispensed to us. There are seven: Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Penance, Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders, and Matrimony.

These seven sacraments touch all the stages and all the important moments of the Christian life: they give birth and growth, healing and mission to the Christian's life of faith. For this reason they can be grouped into three categories: the sacraments of Christian initiation (Baptism, Confirmation, and Eucharist), the sacraments of healing (Penance and Anointing of the Sick), and the sacraments at the service of communion and mission (Holy Orders and Matrimony).

The sacraments act «ex opere operato», that is, by the power of Christ's own action accomplished in them, independently of the personal holiness of the minister — although the fruits also depend on the disposition of the one who receives them. Confirmation catechesis places Confirmation precisely within this whole, as part of the single process of Christian initiation that begins in Baptism.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1113-1134
Second Vatican Council, Constitution Sacrosanctum Concilium, no. 59

itens.titulo: Baptism
itens.resumo: The gateway to the Christian life and to the other sacraments: it wipes away original sin and makes the baptized a child of God and a member of the Church.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in numbers 1213 to 1284, calls Baptism the "gateway to life in the Spirit" and the foundation of the whole Christian life, since without it no other sacrament can be validly received. Through Baptism the Christian is freed from sin, is reborn as a child of God, and becomes a member of Christ, incorporated into the Church.

The essential rite consists of immersing the candidate in water or pouring water on the head, with the invocation of the Most Holy Trinity: "I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit" (cf. Mt 28:19). Like Confirmation and Holy Orders, Baptism imprints on the soul an indelible spiritual character and therefore cannot be repeated.

Saint Paul explains the deepest meaning of this sacrament: "We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead [...], we too might walk in newness of life" (Rom 6:4). Confirmation, normally celebrated after years of baptismal life, is precisely the sacrament that strengthens and brings to maturity this grace received at the beginning.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1213-1284

itens.titulo: The Eucharist and the Holy Mass
itens.resumo: The sacrament in which Christ becomes truly present under the species of bread and wine, the "source and summit" of the whole Christian life.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in numbers 1322 to 1419, teaches that the Eucharist is the "source and summit of the Christian life": in it is contained the whole spiritual good of the Church, namely Christ himself. At the Last Supper, Jesus instituted this sacrament when he said over the bread and the wine, "This is my body... this is my blood," commanding the apostles: "Do this in remembrance of me" (Lk 22:19).

The Church believes and teaches that, through the consecration, the bread and wine truly become the Body and Blood of Christ, with only the appearances of bread and wine remaining, a change that tradition calls transubstantiation. Whoever receives communion is intimately united to Christ and is strengthened in charity and in the struggle against sin.

Numbers 1345 to 1355 describe the structure of the Holy Mass, already recognizable from the first centuries: the gathering of the faithful, the reading of the Word of God, the homily, the presentation of the bread and wine, the Eucharistic prayer of consecration, and communion. Confirmation prepares the confirmand to take part in this celebration with greater awareness and frequency, as the summit of his or her Christian life.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1322-1419, 1345-1355

itens.titulo: Reconciliation and Penance
itens.resumo: The sacrament by which sins committed after Baptism are forgiven through confession and the priest's absolution.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in numbers 1422 to 1498, presents this sacrament under several names that reveal its dimensions: the sacrament of conversion, of confession, of forgiveness, and of reconciliation, for it restores the sinner to communion with God and with the Church.

Its foundation is in Christ himself, who, risen from the dead, said to the apostles: "Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them" (Jn 20:22-23), entrusting to the Church the power to forgive in his name, exercised by bishops and priests.

The acts of the penitent — examination of conscience, contrition, confession to the priest, and satisfaction (penance) — are united to absolution in order to fully restore the grace lost by grave sin and also to reconcile from venial sins. Confirmation catechesis returns to this sacrament so that the candidate for Confirmation, now capable of more mature moral discernment, may learn to turn to it regularly.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1422-1498

itens.titulo: The Anointing of the Sick
itens.resumo: A sacrament that comforts and strengthens the faithful who are gravely ill or elderly, uniting their suffering to that of Christ.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in numbers 1499 to 1532, teaches that the Church received from Christ the mandate to care for the sick and expresses it sacramentally in the Anointing of the Sick, intended for those who begin to be in danger of death from illness or old age. It is one of the two sacraments called "of healing," together with Penance, and its foundation is Jesus' own compassion for the sick, whose healings Scripture presents as a sign that the Kingdom of God has come with Him (CCC 1503-1505).

The biblical foundation is the Letter of James: "Is any among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick man, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven" (Jas 5:14-15). Tradition recognized in this rite one of the seven sacraments (CCC 1510). In the Roman rite, the matter is olive oil — or, according to circumstances, another oil of plant origin — duly blessed, and the form is the anointing of the forehead and hands with the prayer of the priest. The oil of the sick is blessed by the bishop, normally at the Chrism Mass on Holy Thursday, together with the oil of catechumens and the oil of holy Chrism.

The current name is a recent achievement: for centuries the sacrament was called "Extreme Unction" and was administered more and more exclusively to those who were about to die, which obscured its full meaning (CCC 1512). It was the Second Vatican Council that recovered the understanding of the first centuries. The Constitution Sacrosanctum Concilium, the first document promulgated by the Council, states in number 73: "'Extreme unction,' which may also and more fittingly be called 'anointing of the sick,' is not a sacrament for those only who are at the point of death. Hence, as soon as any one of the faithful begins to be in danger of death from sickness or old age, the fitting time for him to receive the sacrament has certainly already arrived." The same document asked for a "continuous rite," in which the anointing is given to the sick person after confession and before the reception of Viaticum (SC 74), and determined that the number of anointings be adapted to the circumstances (SC 75).

The reform was consolidated by the Apostolic Constitution Sacram Unctionem Infirmorum of Paul VI, dated November 30, 1972, which established the new formula: "Through this holy anointing may the Lord in his love and mercy help you with the grace of the Holy Spirit. May the Lord who frees you from sin save you and raise you up" (CCC 1513). The formula makes explicit that the grace conferred is the work of the Holy Spirit and that the sacrament is a remedy for soul and body; because of its penitential efficacy, it can supply for confession when confession is not possible.

This sacrament gives the sick person the grace of the Holy Spirit, which helps him to trust in God, strengthens him against the temptations of discouragement and anguish in the face of death, unites the sick person to the Passion of Christ and, when it is conducive to salvation, restores bodily health (CCC 1520-1523). Whoever is gravely ill should receive the sacrament whenever the illness worsens or recurs, and the faithful may receive it several times throughout life — unlike Baptism, Confirmation and Holy Orders, which imprint an indelible character. When the Anointing is administered to someone close to death, it is completed by the Eucharist, then called Viaticum (from the Latin viaticum, "provisions for the journey"), the Christian's last sacramental food at the passage from this life.

Second Vatican Council, Constitution Sacrosanctum Concilium, nos. 73-75
Paul VI, Apostolic Constitution Sacram Unctionem Infirmorum, November 30, 1972

itens.titulo: The Sacrament of Holy Orders
itens.resumo: The sacrament through which the mission entrusted by Christ to the apostles continues to be exercised in the Church by bishops, priests, and deacons.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in numbers 1536 to 1600, defines Holy Orders as the sacrament through which the mission entrusted by Christ to his apostles continues to be exercised in the Church until the end of time. It comprises three degrees: the episcopate (bishops), the presbyterate (priests), and the diaconate (deacons), each with its own functions in the service of the People of God.

Its essential rite is the laying on of hands by the bishop upon the ordinand, accompanied by the consecratory prayer proper to each degree. Like Baptism and Confirmation, Holy Orders imprints an indelible spiritual character and therefore cannot be repeated.

Bishops, successors of the apostles, receive the fullness of the sacrament; priests are their co-workers, united with them in the priesthood and in the mission of teaching, sanctifying, and governing; deacons are ordained for service, above all that of charity and the liturgy. Confirmation catechesis presents this sacrament among the «sacraments at the service of communion», since it is through it that the Church continues to have those who preside over the other sacraments.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1536-1600
Acts 6:6

itens.titulo: Marriage
itens.resumo: A covenant by which a man and a woman establish between themselves a partnership of life and love, ordered to the good of the spouses and the procreation of children.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in numbers 1601 to 1666, teaches that the matrimonial covenant, by which a man and a woman establish between themselves a partnership of the whole of life, was created and ordered by God for the good of the spouses and for the procreation and education of children; between the baptized, this covenant has been raised by Christ to the dignity of a sacrament.

The free consent of the engaged couple, expressed publicly before the Church, is the element that makes the marriage: "So they are no longer two, but one flesh" (Mt 19:6). This consent establishes a single and indissoluble covenant, open to life.

Conjugal love is called to reflect Christ's love for the Church: "Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the Church" (Eph 5:25). The Confirmation catechesis presents Marriage among the sacraments at the service of communion, as one of the concrete vocations to which the confirmand may, in the future, discern being called.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1601-1666
Eph 5:25

itens.titulo: The Holy Spirit in the Sacramental Life of the Church
itens.resumo: The Holy Spirit's own action in every liturgical celebration, making the mystery of Christ present and effective in the sacraments.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in nos. 1091 to 1109, teaches that in every liturgical action the Holy Spirit is sent to accomplish what the Word proclaims: he prepares the assembly to encounter Christ, recalls and manifests the mystery of Christ to it, makes this mystery present and actual, and unites the Church to the life and mission of Christ.

This action finds its most visible expression in the epiclesis — the invocation of the Holy Spirit upon the assembly, the gifts, and the ministers — present in all the sacraments: it is the Spirit who, when invoked, makes the bread and wine the Body and Blood of Christ, who consecrates the oil of chrism, who makes every absolution and every anointing effective.

Just as Jesus, after his resurrection, breathed on the apostles saying "Receive the Holy Spirit" (Jn 20:22), each sacrament is an occasion of a new gift of the same Spirit, given in a culminating way in Confirmation, whose very rite, by anointing the forehead of the confirmand with holy chrism, visibly expresses this outpouring.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1091-1109

itens.titulo: The Sponsor in Confirmation (Godfather and Godmother)
itens.resumo: The one who accompanies the candidate before and after the celebration, helping him or her to live in accord with the faith received and to persevere in the Christian life.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in number 1311, teaches that, in order to receive Confirmation, it is appropriate to have a sponsor, whose role is to take care that the confirmand behaves as a true witness of Christ and faithfully fulfills the obligations connected with this sacrament. For this reason the Church recommends that, whenever possible, the same godfather or godmother as at Baptism be sought, in order to preserve the unity of this mission.

Numbers 1309 and 1310 also recall that preparation for Confirmation should lead the candidate to a more intimate union with Christ and a greater familiarity with the Holy Spirit — his gifts and his action — and awakens a sense of belonging to the Church, both universal and parochial. It is along this path that the role of the sponsor is concretely exercised.

More than a title of honor, the sponsor takes on, before God and the community, a commitment: to accompany the candidate with a witness of faith and spiritual friendship, especially in the years following the celebration, when the young Christian's life choices begin to mature.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1309-1311
Paul VI, Apostolic Constitution «Divinae consortium naturae» (1971)

itens.titulo: The Symbols of the Rite of Confirmation
itens.resumo: The oil of holy chrism and the laying on of hands, signs by which the bishop conveys the gift of the Holy Spirit to the person being confirmed.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in nos. 1293 to 1301, explains the meaning of the signs used in the celebration of Confirmation. Anointing with oil has, in Sacred Scripture and in ancient tradition, a rich meaning: it signifies abundance, joy, healing, the strengthening of the muscles of athletes and wrestlers, and a sign of beauty, health and strength.

The oil used specifically is holy chrism, oil mixed with balsam, consecrated by the bishop, usually at the Chrism Mass on Holy Thursday, and therefore reserved solely for this use. To anoint someone with it means to mark them with the "seal" of the Holy Spirit, a sign of belonging to Christ, of promised fidelity and of mission received (cf. Acts 8:17, where the apostles laid their hands on them and the Holy Spirit was given).

Nos. 1312 to 1314 recall that the original minister of this rite is the Bishop, successor of the apostles, which manifests the bond of the person being confirmed with the apostolic and universal Church; in circumstances determined by the law of the Church, the bishop may grant a priest the faculty to administer this sacrament.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1293-1301, 1312-1314
Acts 8:17

itens.titulo: The Forms of Christian Prayer
itens.resumo: Vocal prayer, meditation, and contemplation: the three main expressions by which Christians unite themselves to God in faith.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in nos. 2700 to 2724, presents three major forms of prayer, all present in the lives of the saints and recommended by Tradition. Vocal prayer joins the body to the interior prayer of the heart, giving it words — from the simplest formulas to the great prayers of the liturgy — and it is indispensable even for those who have already attained higher degrees of prayer.

Meditation is a quest: it engages thought, imagination, emotion, and desire, in order to deepen faith, convert the heart, and strengthen the will to follow Christ, often taking as its support the reading of Scripture or of spiritual texts.

Contemplation, for its part, is defined by the Catechism, following Saint Teresa of Avila, as «a gaze of faith fixed on Jesus», a time of silence and love before God, without many words. The three forms are not mutually exclusive: they fulfill Saint Paul's command — «pray without ceasing» (1 Thess 5:17) —, a goal that Confirmation catechesis sets before the confirmand as a journey to be traveled, and not as a point of arrival.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 2700-2724
1 Thess 5:17

itens.titulo: The Our Father in the Christian Life
itens.resumo: The prayer that Jesus himself taught his disciples, a summary of the whole Gospel, prayed at the center of the Church's liturgy.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in numbers 2759 to 2865, calls the Our Father the «summary of the whole Gospel», the perfect prayer taught by Jesus when the disciples asked him: «Lord, teach us to pray» (Lk 11:1). Composed of seven petitions, it is directed first to the glory of the Father — his name, his Kingdom, his will — and then to human needs — daily bread, forgiveness, and protection from temptation and evil.

By calling God «Father», the Christian recognizes himself as an adopted child, able to address him with the same filial trust as Jesus; the word «our» reminds us that this prayer is never made in an individualistic way, but always in communion with the whole Church and with all humanity.

For this reason the Our Father holds a central place in the liturgy: it is prayed at every Mass, before communion, and at many other sacramental moments and in personal prayer. Confirmation catechesis takes up this prayer again so that the confirmand may understand it not only by heart, but in its theological and spiritual meaning.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 2759-2865

itens.titulo: The First Commandment: Loving God Above All Things
itens.resumo: To adore God alone by the virtue of religion, distinguishing latria, dulia and hyperdulia, and to avoid idolatry and superstition.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in numbers 2084 to 2141, explains the first commandment — "I am the Lord your God [...] you shall have no other gods before me" (Ex 20:2-3) — as the foundation of all the others. The text opens by recalling not a prohibition, but an action of God: "I am the one who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery" (Dt 5:6); the commandment arises from a God who first liberates and then asks for fidelity. The Catechism classifies the central requirement as belonging to the virtue of religion, which disposes man to acknowledge God as Creator and Lord and to render him the worship due to him (CCC 2084-2086, 2095-2096).

The rigorous Catholic tradition distinguishes three degrees of worship, a distinction the Catechism takes up: latria (adoration), owed exclusively to God — "Adoration is the first act of the virtue of religion," teaches CCC 2096 —; dulia (veneration), rendered to the saints and angels, by reason of God's grace in them; and hyperdulia, a singular veneration reserved to the Virgin Mary for her unique mission as Mother of God. This difference is not a late scholastic refinement, but the key to understanding why honor given to images and to the saints does not constitute idolatry: the honor paid to an image passes to the prototype it represents, and not to the material thing as such (CCC 2131-2132). The Catechism also recalls that "the veneration of sacred images is based on the mystery of the Incarnation of the Word of God. It is not contrary to the first commandment" (CCC 2141).

Opposed to this commandment are, on the one hand, sins by deficiency of religion — unbelief, heresy, apostasy, schism and despair — and, on the other, sins by deformed excess, such as superstition, idolatry — putting creatures, idols or powers in the place of God — and magic or divination (CCC 2110-2117). The Catechism is precise in describing superstition: it is the deviation that can affect even legitimate practices, for example when an efficacy that is "in some way magical" is attributed to prayers or sacramental signs, independently of the interior dispositions (CCC 2111). Idolatry, for its part, condemns above all polytheism: Sacred Scripture rejects it as worship of "the work of human hands" (cf. Ps 115:4-5).

There is also a historical point that the Catechism records: the division and numbering of the commandments have varied throughout history. The current text follows the division established by Saint Augustine, who grouped Ex 20:3-6 into a single commandment and split Ex 20:17 into two (against coveting one's neighbor's wife and against other forms of covetousness) — a division that is also that of the Lutheran confessions. The Greek Fathers made a different division, followed in the Orthodox Churches and in the Reformed communities (CCC 2066). This means that what Catholics call the "first commandment" corresponds, for example, to the first two in a Protestant numbering. CCC 2067 observes that the first three commandments refer more to the love of God and the following seven to the love of neighbor, and that the words of the Decalogue, far from being abolished, "received amplification and development" with the coming of Christ.

Jesus himself summed up this commandment by quoting the Book of Deuteronomy — "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the great and first commandment" (Mt 22:37-38, cf. Dt 6:5) — and rebuffed the temptation in the desert by answering with the exclusive adoration of God: "You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve" (Mt 4:10). On this foundation the Confirmation catechesis builds its whole understanding of the Christian moral life.

itens.titulo: The Second Commandment: Respecting the Name of God
itens.resumo: Using God's name with reverence, avoiding blasphemy, false or unnecessary oaths, and every abuse of the sacred.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in numbers 2142 to 2167, teaches that the second commandment — "You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain" (Ex 20:7) — calls for respect for the name of God, which in biblical faith reveals the very identity and presence of the one who bears it.

Blasphemy (words of hatred, reproach, or defiance against God), a false oath or one taken lightly, and the misuse of God's name for magical or manipulative purposes all sin against this commandment. The name of Jesus, of Mary, and of the saints also deserves this same respect.

The Catechism also recalls that Christians receive their own name in Baptism, often that of a saint, who becomes a protector and a model of charity; and that God's name is sanctified in the world above all by the holy life of Christians, a truth that Confirmation catechesis associates with the first petition of the Our Father, "hallowed be thy name."
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 2142-2167

itens.titulo: The Third Commandment: Keeping the Lord's Day Holy
itens.resumo: Keeping Sunday as the Lord's Day by taking part in Mass and living rest as a sign of the freedom of the children of God.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in nos. 2168 to 2195, explains that the third commandment — "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy" (Ex 20:8) — gathers up the biblical precept of the Sabbath rest and transfers it, in the Christian tradition, to Sunday, the day on which Christ rose from the dead. The reason for the change is theological and not merely disciplinary: Sunday (from the Latin dies dominica, "the Lord's day") is the weekly Easter, the living memorial of the Resurrection.

The oldest testimony to this practice dates from the middle of the second century. In his First Apology, Saint Justin Martyr († c. 165) describes: "On the day called the day of the sun, all who live in cities or in the country gather together in one place, and the memoirs of the Apostles or the writings of the Prophets are read... and the Eucharist is distributed and received." Sunday does not arise, therefore, from a late decision, but from the apostolic awareness that Easter fulfills the Sabbath.

The Catechism (nos. 2180-2181) specifies the duty of the Eucharistic precept: "On Sundays and other holy days of obligation, the faithful are bound to participate in the Mass," and "those who deliberately fail in this obligation commit a grave sin." The Code of Canon Law (can. 1247) confirms the same norm as universal law, and the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches (can. 881 § 1) prescribes an analogous obligation for the Divine Liturgy. The duty also falls upon Pastors, who must "offer everyone the effective possibility of fulfilling the precept."

The doctrine was taken up systematically by Pope John Paul II in the Apostolic Letter Dies Domini, of May 31, 1998, on keeping the Lord's Day holy. In it the Pope distinguishes three dimensions of the day: Sunday is the "primordial feast" that reveals the meaning of time and the Resurrection of Christ, it is the day of the Eucharistic assembly — the "heart of Sunday" — and it is the day of solidarity and rest. He further insists that Sunday should not be experienced merely as a precept, but as a requirement inscribed in Christian existence: one "cannot live out one's faith, in full participation in the life of the Christian community, without regularly taking part in the Sunday Eucharistic assembly."

Sunday rest, therefore, is neither mere physical rest nor a simple interruption of work, but an expression of the freedom of the children of God: time given for family life, culture, charity and above all prayer. It is in this sense that Confirmation catechesis insists on the confirmand's regular participation in Sunday Mass, as a concrete sign of belonging to the community of the baptized.

itens.titulo: The Fourth Commandment: Honor Your Father and Mother
itens.resumo: The reciprocal duties between parents and children, and the respect also owed to the other legitimate forms of authority.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in nos. 2197 to 2257, teaches that the fourth commandment — "Honor your father and your mother" (Ex 20:12) — governs the closest relationships of human communion and asks children for respect, gratitude, just obedience, and assistance to their parents, especially in sickness and old age.

By extension, the Catechism applies this commandment to every legitimate relationship of authority within the human community: between students and teachers, employees and employers, citizens and their country. Civil authority, when exercised with respect for human dignity and the common good, also deserves obedience, within the limits of the moral law.

Parents, for their part, have the grave duty to care for the human and Christian education of their children, being the first persons responsible for them and their first educators in the faith, a duty that Confirmation catechesis explicitly recognizes by counting on the collaboration of the family in the preparation of the confirmand.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 2197-2257

itens.titulo: The Fifth Commandment: You Shall Not Kill
itens.resumo: The respect owed to human life, from conception to natural death, and to the health and dignity of every person, according to the Catechism (nos. 2258-2330).
itens.corpo:
The Catechism of the Catholic Church treats the fifth commandment in numbers 2258 to 2330, opening the section with the affirmation that human life is sacred from its beginning to its natural end, because it involves the creative action of God and remains forever in a special relationship with Him, "who is the sole Lord of life." Saint John Paul II takes up this same formulation in the encyclical Evangelium vitae (1995), no. 53, linking it to Genesis 1 and to the commandment "You shall not kill" (Ex 20:13; Deut 5:17). The biblical commandment is therefore read in the light of the creation of man in the image of God and of his vocation to eternal communion — which grounds the inviolability of every human life, including that of the criminal.

The conciliar text and the Catechism organize the subject around direct and voluntary homicide (no. 2268), which forbids killing as gravely sinful and names as especially grave crimes infanticide, fratricide, parricide, and the murder of a spouse — without "concerns of eugenics or public hygiene" being able to justify any homicide. No. 2269 further forbids indirectly causing death, obliging one to help those in danger and describing the acceptance of deadly famines as a "scandalous injustice" and a grave sin. From this principle derive the teachings on direct abortion (nos. 2270-2273), which the Church punishes with the canonical penalty of excommunication, and on the defense of the embryo, which "must be treated as a person from conception"; on euthanasia (no. 2324), defined as homicide "gravely contrary to the dignity of the human person"; and on suicide (nos. 2280-2283), which is contrary to justice, hope, and charity.

The excommunication attached to abortion is not a metaphor: the 1983 Code of Canon Law, in canon 1398, determines that "a person who procures a completed abortion incurs a latae sententiae excommunication" — an automatic penalty, applied at the very moment of the offense, without need of a declaratory sentence. It reaches all who cooperate materially or morally in the procedure, although canon 1324 provides for mitigation in circumstances such as coercion by grave fear. The same section of the Catechism deals with legitimate defense, which is lawful provided that the means employed is proportionate and is not deliberately directed against the aggressor, and with capital punishment.

Concerning the latter, there has been a recent and much-discussed doctrinal change. The earlier text of no. 2267 admitted recourse to the death penalty as "an acceptable, though extreme, means for the protection of the common good." On August 2, 2018, Pope Francis approved, by means of a rescript, a new wording (the text was approved at the audience of May 11, 2018 granted to the then prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Cardinal Luis Ladaria). The new version teaches that "the death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person," and the Church "works with determination for its abolition worldwide." In the letter to the bishops, Cardinal Ladaria presented the text as an "authentic development of doctrine," not a contradiction of the earlier Magisterium. The formulation did not escape controversy: some theologians and prelates contested the change, questioning its coherence with traditional teaching, which shows how the fifth commandment continues to be the subject of lively theological debate.

The commandment also requires, according to the Catechism, care for one's own health and that of others, respect for the bodies of the deceased, and the building of peace, avoiding anger, hatred, scandal, and violence, and it condemns war except under the conditions of legitimate defense. For Confirmation catechesis, the fifth commandment is presented as the foundation of all Christian social ethics: it starts from concrete personal decisions of the young confirmand (respect for one's own life and that of one's neighbor) and extends to the great questions of justice that the Church faces in the contemporary world.

itens.titulo: The Sixth Commandment: You Shall Not Commit Adultery
itens.resumo: Chastity as the virtue that integrates human sexuality into the person, and the fidelity owed to the marriage bond.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in numbers 2331 to 2400, teaches that human sexuality touches the most intimate dimensions of the person and of the couple, and that God created it as a good to be lived with respect for one's own dignity and that of others, within the total gift of self expressed in marriage.

The sixth commandment — "You shall not commit adultery" (Ex 20:14) — protects above all conjugal fidelity, but the tradition of the Church understands it more broadly as a call to chastity, a virtue that harmoniously integrates sexuality into the whole person, whether in marriage or in the celibate or single life.

Chastity is not the absence of sexuality, but an interior mastery that is learned progressively, with the grace of God and personal effort, aided by friendship, prayer and the sacraments — a concrete challenge that Confirmation catechesis proposes to the young candidate for Confirmation as a path of freedom and affective maturity.

itens.titulo: The Seventh Commandment: You Shall Not Steal
itens.resumo: Respect for the goods of others and for legitimate property, ordered to the universal destination of goods, to social justice, and to a just wage.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in numbers 2401 to 2463, explains that the seventh commandment — "You shall not steal" (Ex 20:15) — forbids unjustly taking or keeping the goods of one's neighbor and prescribes the practice of justice and charity in the management of earthly goods and the fruits of human labor (CCC 2401, 2451). Theft is precisely defined as "the usurpation of another's property against the reasonable will of the owner" (CCC 2453); but the Catechism distinguishes theft from what is not theft: there is no theft if consent can be presumed or if refusal is contrary to reason and the universal destination of goods, as in the case of urgent and obvious necessity, where the only way to provide for immediate, essential needs — food, shelter, clothing — is to dispose of and use another's property (CCC 2408).

The Catechism lists what violates this commandment: deliberately keeping goods lent or objects lost; committing fraud in business; paying unjust wages; raising prices by taking advantage of the ignorance or hardship of others; speculation by which the value of goods is artificially manipulated in order to gain an advantage to the detriment of others; and corruption that influences the judgment of those who must make legal decisions (CCC 2409). It also stresses that creation was given by God to all humanity: "the goods of creation are destined for the entire human race. The right to private property does not abolish the universal destination of goods" (CCC 2452). Legitimate property is protected, but subordinated to the common good: whoever possesses more has a special responsibility to share.

This teaching belongs to the Church's Social Doctrine, inaugurated by the encyclical Rerum Novarum of Leo XIII, published on May 15, 1891, in response to the Industrial Revolution and the labor question. Leo XIII affirmed that "private ownership is a natural right of man" (RN 5), but rejected both socialism, which proposed the abolition of private property, and unregulated capitalism, which exploited workers. From Rerum Novarum comes the principle of the just wage: the worker should not receive less than what is sufficient to support himself, his wife, and his children (cf. RN 45). The Second Vatican Council took up the theme in the Constitution Gaudium et Spes (1965), which treats "earthly goods as destined for all" (GS 69) and recalls that "whatever the forms of ownership may be, one must always pay attention to this universal destination of goods" (GS 69). John Paul II deepened it in Laborem Exercens (1981), insisting that human labor has priority over capital and that the person is the subject, and not the instrument, of work.

The seventh commandment therefore includes demands that go beyond individual theft: the duty to work honestly, to practice social justice, to respect the integrity of creation, and to practice sobriety. Confirmation catechesis takes up these principles by proposing to the confirmand a sober and supportive way of life, attentive to the doctrine of the universal destination of goods and to the principle that material goods are means, and not ends, of the human vocation.

itens.titulo: The Eighth Commandment: You Shall Not Bear False Witness
itens.resumo: The commitment to truth, honesty, and respect for people's reputation, honor, and privacy, with decisive applications in the use of digital networks.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in nos. 2464 to 2513, teaches that the eighth commandment — "You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor" (Ex 20:16) — forbids misrepresenting the truth in our relations with others. This moral prescription flows from the vocation of the people of God to bear witness to the God who is the truth and wills the truth (CCC 2464). The Deuteronomic form of the commandment is more developed: "Neither shall you bear false witness against your neighbor" (Dt 5:20), placing it in the context of a covenant that demands truthfulness in words and deeds.

The Catechism carefully distinguishes offenses against the truth. A person is guilty of "false witness" who, in court, states the contrary of the truth; of "perjury" who does so under oath (CCC 2476). In the broader sphere of daily life, CCC 2477 distinguishes: rash judgment, when one assumes as true, without sufficient foundation, the moral fault of a neighbor; detraction, when one, without objectively valid reason, discloses another's faults and failings to persons who did not know them; and calumny, when, by remarks contrary to the truth, one harms the reputation of others and gives occasion for false judgments concerning them. The Catechism recalls that everything done against the truth is also an offense against the right to honor, a good "more precious than riches" (CCC 2479). Against rash judgment, it prescribes a favorable interpretation of the neighbor: "Every good Christian ought to be more ready to give a favorable interpretation to another's statement than to condemn it" (CCC 2478, following Saint Ignatius of Loyola).

The Catechism also protects the keeping of confidences. The sacramental seal of Reconciliation "is inviolable; accordingly, it is a crime for a confessor in any way to betray a penitent by word or in any manner and for any reason" (CCC 2490, citing the Code of Canon Law). Professional secrets — known, for example, to physicians, jurists, or politicians — must likewise be kept, except in exceptional cases where keeping the secret would cause very grave harm that can be avoided only by revealing the truth (CCC 2491).

The Magisterium's entry into the subject of the media is explicit: the Decree Inter Mirifica of the Second Vatican Council, promulgated by Paul VI on December 4, 1963, was the first conciliar document to deal with the press, cinema, radio, and television, affirming society's right to information based on truth, freedom, and justice (CCC 2512). The Catechism concludes the article by linking truth to beauty: the fine arts, and above all sacred art, should evoke and glorify the mystery of God revealed in Christ (CCC 2513). Applied today to digital networks — where false information can harm a person's reputation within minutes and reach an immense audience — the commandment asks the confirmand for sobriety in speech, responsibility in sharing, and active refusal of online defamation.
