itens.titulo: The Ninth Commandment: You Shall Not Covet Your Neighbor's Wife
itens.resumo: The purification of the heart and the fight against carnal concupiscence, a condition for living chastity in its fullness and for "seeing God."
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in numbers 2514 to 2533, teaches that the ninth commandment asks for the purification of the heart and combats the concupiscence of the flesh: it is not enough to avoid external sin; one must keep watch over the thoughts and desires that precede it. The starting point is the Johannine distinction of the three kinds of covetousness or concupiscence: "the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life" (1 Jn 2:16). According to the Catholic catechetical tradition, the ninth commandment forbids carnal concupiscence, while the tenth has as its object the coveting of the goods of others (CCC 2514). It is worth noting that, etymologically, "concupiscence" can designate every vehement form of human desire; it is not in itself a sin, but a disordered tendency that becomes sinful when it is consented to (CCC 2515).

The foundation is the word of Jesus: "Everyone who looks at a woman with lust has already committed adultery with her in his heart" (Mt 5:28). The battle for purity is therefore fought first in the interior of the person, and the Catechism summarizes it in the formula "the struggle against carnal covetousness entails purifying the heart and practicing temperance" (CCC 2530). Saint John presents purity of heart as a condition for the vision of God: the pure of heart "shall see God" (cf. Mt 5:8), and from now on they see all things according to God (CCC 2519, 2531).

The means of this purification are concrete and listed by the Catechism: prayer, the practice of chastity, which is a virtue and a gift of God, purity of intention and of outward and inward vision, and the discipline of the senses and the imagination (CCC 2520, 2532). The Compendium adds that the baptized person, with the grace of God, in struggle against disordered desires, attains purity of heart by these paths (Compendium, no. 529). Associated with this purification is modesty, which "protects the intimate center of the person" and is patience, decency, and discretion in speech, dress, and action (CCC 2521-2523, 2533).

Confirmation catechesis treats this commandment as a continuation of the sixth, insisting that chastity is the fruit of continuous interior work and not of a single decision; it does not deny the value of human attraction, but orders the affections according to each person's own vocation: to marriage, to consecrated life, or to celibacy. In societies saturated with images and erotic stimuli, the ninth commandment recalls that purity is also built socially, requiring a purification of customs and responsibility on the part of those who produce and spread content.

itens.titulo: The Tenth Commandment: You Shall Not Covet Your Neighbor's Goods
itens.resumo: Detachment of the heart from material goods, poverty of spirit, and the struggle against covetousness and envy as a path to interior freedom.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in nos. 2534 to 2557, explains that the tenth commandment completes the ninth: whereas the ninth concerns concupiscence of the flesh, the tenth forbids coveting the goods of others, the "root of the theft, robbery, and fraud" forbidden by the seventh commandment (CCC 2534). The biblical text — "You shall not covet your neighbor's house; ... or his ox, or his ass, or anything that is your neighbor's" (Ex 20:17) — is inscribed on the two tablets of the Law, and the catechetical tradition has already distinguished, following Saint John, three kinds of concupiscence: "the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life" (1 Jn 2:16), present in CCC 2514.

The distinction from the preceding commandment is precise: the ninth forbids disordered desire for the person of one's neighbor; the tenth, disordered desire for his things. The Catechism observes that covetousness, "like fornication, has its origin in idolatry," prohibited in the first three prescriptions of the Law (CCC 2534) — that is, disordered attachment to money conceals a false worship. For this reason no. 2536 condemns "greed and the desire for an immoderate appropriation of earthly goods" and "unrestrained avarice, born of the immoderate passion for riches and their power."

The commandment requires that envy be banished from the heart. The Catechism recalls, as a warning, the episode in which the prophet Nathan exposes King David with the parable of the poor man who had only one ewe lamb, coveted by the rich man (2 Sam 12) (CCC 2538). Envy, defined as sadness at the good of another and the immoderate desire to possess it unduly, is counted among the capital sins (CCC 2539), and from it are born hatred, detraction, calumny, and joy at another's misfortune. In this sense, avarice — which Hugh of Saint Victor described as the vice that "throws man to the ground" and which Saint Thomas Aquinas analyzes as an immoderate desire that exceeds the measure necessary for human life — is among the seven capital sins (CCC 1866).

Jesus shows where the root of everything lies: "Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also" (Mt 6:21). Hence the radical formula that Confirmation catechesis takes up: "You cannot serve God and mammon" (Mt 6:24). The response to the tenth commandment, according to the Catechism (nos. 2544-2547), is not merely abstention, but the virtue of poverty of heart — "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (Mt 5:3) — by which the disciple rightly orders his affections and makes God his only treasure, an attitude that Confirmation associates directly with the first of the Beatitudes.

itens.titulo: The Beatitudes
itens.resumo: The heart of Jesus' preaching in the Sermon on the Mount: a path of true happiness that portrays the very face of Christ.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in numbers 1716 to 1729, presents the Beatitudes as the summary of Jesus' moral teaching, proclaimed at the beginning of the Sermon on the Mount: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, [...] those who mourn, [...] the meek, [...] those who hunger and thirst for righteousness..." (Mt 5:3-12).

Each beatitude promises a happiness that is paradoxical in the eyes of the world — associating true joy with poverty, suffering, meekness, mercy, purity of heart, the pursuit of peace, and even persecution for the sake of righteousness — responding to the natural desire for happiness that every human being carries within, but directing it toward God as the only good that can fully satisfy it.

The Beatitudes portray the very face of Jesus Christ and describe his charity; they are also, according to the Catechism, a light that guides the Christian's actions amid the concrete circumstances of life, including those that Confirmation catechesis helps young people discern in their own lives.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1716-1729

itens.titulo: The Moral Law and Conscience
itens.resumo: The natural law inscribed in the heart of every human being, and conscience as the practical judgment that applies it to each concrete action.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in nos. 1950 to 1974, teaches that there is a natural moral law, an expression of the wisdom and goodness of God, inscribed in the heart of every human being and recognizable by reason: «Saint Paul says that the Gentiles [...] show that the law is written in their hearts» (cf. Rom 2:14-16). This natural law finds its historical expression in the Old Law (the Decalogue) and its fullness in the New Law, the Gospel of Christ, summed up in the commandment of love.

Moral conscience, treated in nos. 1776 to 1802, is defined as a «judgment of reason» by which the person recognizes the moral quality of a concrete act that he is about to perform, is in the process of performing, or has already performed: it is the «voice» that invites to good and turns away from evil in each particular situation of life.

Conscience must be continually formed by the Word of God, by the teaching of the Church, and by sincere examination of oneself, since it can err through non-culpable ignorance or through culpable negligence. To discern with a upright conscience, according to the moral law received from God, is a task that Confirmation catechesis helps the young person take on with greater autonomy and responsibility.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1776-1802, 1950-1974

itens.titulo: Sin: Original, Mortal, and Venial
itens.resumo: The inherited condition of rupture with God transmitted by Adam, and the personal sins that either break or merely wound the divine friendship.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in paragraphs 396 to 421, teaches that, through the sin of our first parents, humanity lost its original harmony with God, with itself, and with creation: this condition, inherited by every human being at birth and not a personal act, is called original sin. Saint Paul sums it up: "Sin came into the world through one man" (Rom 5:12).

The Catechism, in paragraphs 1846 to 1876, then distinguishes personal sins, freely committed by each individual: mortal sin destroys charity in the heart of man by a grave violation of the law of God, involving grave matter, full knowledge, and deliberate consent, and causes the loss of the life of grace; venial sin weakens charity without breaking the covenant with God, being a less serious disorder that nonetheless deserves purification.

This teaching is not meant to generate paralyzing guilt, but to offer a realistic path of conversion: the same God who reveals the gravity of sin offers, in Baptism and in the sacrament of Reconciliation, the forgiveness and grace needed to begin again — a truth that Confirmation catechesis takes up as it prepares young people for a mature moral life.

itens.titulo: Grace
itens.resumo: God's free and supernatural help, which justifies us, makes us adopted children, and makes us sharers in the divine life itself.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in numbers 1996 to 2005, defines grace as "favor, the free and undeserved help that God gives us to respond to his call" to become adopted children, partakers of the divine nature and of eternal life (cf. Eph 2:8-9). It is not something that human beings can merit by their own merits; it is an absolutely free gift.

Habitual, or sanctifying, grace is that permanent disposition which makes us able to live and to act according to the divine call, healing and sanctifying human nature wounded by sin. Alongside it there are also actual graces, occasional gifts of God for concrete acts of conversion or sanctification, and sacramental and charismatic graces, proper to each sacrament or gift received.

Life in grace is, at the same time, gift and responsibility: it demands the free cooperation of the person, nourished by prayer and the sacraments. Confirmation, in a special way, is presented by the tradition of the Church as an increase and deepening of baptismal grace, strengthening the union of the candidate for Confirmation with Christ and with the Church.

itens.titulo: The Theological and Cardinal Virtues
itens.resumo: Faith, hope, and charity directly orient the Christian toward God; prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance dispose one to act well.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in nos. 1812 to 1829, presents the theological virtues—faith, hope, and charity—as the foundation and dynamism of Christian moral action, infused by God into the soul to make the Christian capable of acting as His child. Faith is adherence to God and to the truth He has revealed; hope trusts in the promised eternal life and in the help of the Holy Spirit; charity, the greatest of the three (cf. 1 Cor 13:13), is the love of God above all things and of neighbor as oneself.

The cardinal virtues, treated in nos. 1804 to 1811, are stable dispositions acquired by human effort, though purified and elevated by grace: prudence disposes reason to discern, in every circumstance, our true good; justice leads one to give God and neighbor what is their due; fortitude ensures firmness in difficulties and constancy in the pursuit of the good; temperance moderates the attraction of pleasures and maintains balance in the use of goods.

These seven virtues—three theological and four cardinal—form, according to the tradition of the Church, the core of every mature moral life, and Confirmation catechesis presents them as the soil in which the gifts of the Holy Spirit, received in the sacrament, find fertile ground to grow.

itens.titulo: The Seven Capital Sins
itens.resumo: Pride, avarice, envy, wrath, lust, gluttony, and sloth: deeply rooted vices that generate and feed other sins.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in treating sin at number 1866, recalls that the spiritual tradition of the Church, taking up the Roman Catechism, distinguishes vices according to the virtues they oppose or, more specifically, according to the seven capital sins: pride, avarice, envy, wrath, lust, gluttony, and sloth — also called acedia.

They are called «capital» because, like a head (caput, in Latin), they generate and command other sins and other vices: pride, for example, distorts the relationship with God and with others, whereas spiritual sloth can lead to the abandonment of the life of prayer and of Christian duties.

The recognition of these vices does not seek to generate scrupulosity, but to help Christians discern, in the examination of conscience, the deepest roots of their own sins, so as to combat them through the practice of the opposite virtues — a theme that Confirmation catechesis takes up together with the teaching on conscience and on the sacrament of Reconciliation.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 1866

itens.titulo: The Works of Mercy
itens.resumo: Corporal and spiritual actions by which the Christian assists a neighbor in need, in imitation of God's mercy.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in number 2447, teaches that the works of mercy are charitable actions by which we come to the aid of our neighbor in their bodily and spiritual necessities, and it lists them according to tradition: feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, welcoming the stranger, caring for the sick and the imprisoned, and burying the dead are the corporal works of mercy; instructing, advising, consoling, comforting, forgiving, and bearing wrongs patiently are the spiritual works of mercy.

These works find their direct foundation in Jesus' words about the Last Judgment: "I was hungry and you gave me food [...]; as you did it to one of the least of these my brethren, you did it to me" (Mt 25:35, 40), a passage in which Christ identifies himself with those who suffer.

Within preparation for Confirmation, many dioceses and parishes ask the candidate for Confirmation to perform some concrete act of service to their neighbor, precisely so that the faith professed in catechesis classes may be translated into lived charitable action, according to the spirit of these works.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 2447

itens.titulo: The Christian Vocation and the States of Life
itens.resumo: Every baptized person is called to holiness; this common vocation is fulfilled in different ways — as a lay person, an ordained minister, or a consecrated person.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in paragraphs 871 to 913, teaches that all the faithful, by being baptized, share in their own way in the priestly, prophetic, and kingly office of Christ. Among them, the lay faithful have as their specific vocation to seek the Kingdom of God by engaging in temporal affairs and ordering them according to God, bearing witness to Christ in the midst of the ordinary tasks of life.

In paragraphs 914 to 933, the Catechism treats consecrated life, in which persons commit themselves, by vows or promises, to follow Christ more closely, living the evangelical counsels of poverty, chastity, and obedience in institutes approved by the Church — a prophetic sign that the Kingdom of God has already begun.

To these forms of life is added the sacrament of Holy Orders, which confers on the man called to ordained ministry a specific mission of service to the community. Saint Paul reminds us that "there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit [...] To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good" (1 Cor 12:4, 7): Confirmation catechesis invites young people to begin discerning to which of these concrete paths God is calling them.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 871-913, 914-933

itens.titulo: The Evangelizing Mission of the Church
itens.resumo: The Church is sent by Christ to proclaim the Gospel to all nations, a task in which each baptized person has a share of their own.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in paragraphs 849 to 856, teaches that the Church is missionary by her very nature, since she draws her origin from the mission of the Son and the mission of the Holy Spirit, according to the plan of God the Father. The mandate was given by the risen Christ himself: "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Mt 28:19).

This mission is born of the love with which God loves all people and of the desire that all come to the knowledge of the truth and be saved; for this reason the Church cannot fail to proclaim the Gospel, always respecting the freedom of each person and engaging in dialogue with different cultures and religions.

Evangelizing is not a task reserved to priests, bishops or missionaries sent to distant lands: every Christian, by the power of Baptism and Confirmation, receives a share in this mission, in the concrete setting in which he or she lives—family, school, work, friendships—following the mandate of Mark 16:15: "Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to the whole creation."
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 849-856

itens.titulo: The Chrism Mass and the Blessing of the Holy Chrism
itens.resumo: On the morning of Holy Thursday, the bishop consecrates the Holy Chrism and blesses the oils that will be used in the sacraments throughout the year.
itens.corpo:
Every year, on the morning of Holy Thursday, the bishop gathers the clergy of the entire diocese in the cathedral to celebrate the Chrism Mass, also called the Mass of the Holy Oils. In it, the oil of catechumens, used in preparation for Baptism, and the oil of the sick, used in the Anointing of the Sick, are blessed; and the Holy Chrism is consecrated, a perfumed oil that will be used throughout the entire year for the anointings of Baptism, Confirmation, and priestly and episcopal Ordination in the whole diocese.

The Catechism recalls, in number 1297, that this Mass commemorates the consecration of the holy oils and usually precedes the Paschal Triduum. In the same celebration, the priests present publicly renew the promises made on the day of their ordination, a gesture that visibly unites the whole presbyterate around their bishop.

The Chrism consecrated at this Mass is then distributed to the parishes and kept there with honor, to be used throughout the year at every Baptism and every Confirmation celebrated in the diocese — which makes the anointing received by the person being confirmed part of a single oil consecrated by the whole people of God gathered around their bishop.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 1297

itens.titulo: The Age of Confirmation
itens.resumo: The Latin tradition links Confirmation to the "age of discretion," but the concrete age has varied throughout history and still changes today depending on the diocese.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism teaches, in number 1307, that the Latin custom, for centuries, has pointed to the "age of discretion" as the reference for Confirmation, traditionally understood as the completed seventh year — although in danger of death a child should be confirmed even before that. The 1983 Code of Canon Law, in canon 891, maintains this reference, but allows each episcopal conference to determine another age, which has made the practice vary considerably from country to country.

The age of Confirmation has been different in other periods: the Roman Catechism, published in 1566 after the Council of Trent, taught that it should be conferred around the age of seven, and the 1917 Code of Canon Law maintained this same guideline. Throughout the twentieth century, however, it became common in many countries to postpone Confirmation to pre-adolescence or adolescence, between ten and sixteen years of age, in order to allow for a longer catechesis before the sacrament.

The Catechism warns, in number 1308, against confusing the "adult age of faith" with the adult age of natural growth: baptismal grace is already a free and full gift, which does not need "ratification" to become effective. Confirmation is therefore not a prize for maturity attained, but a new gift of the Holy Spirit that deepens a grace already received in Baptism.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1307-1308
Code of Canon Law (1983), can. 891
Roman Catechism (1566)

itens.titulo: Confirmation in the Eastern Churches
itens.resumo: In the Eastern Churches, even the Catholic ones, Chrismation is given immediately after Baptism, even when the person baptized is an infant.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism observes, in number 1233, that in the Eastern rites the Christian initiation of infants begins with Baptism followed immediately by Confirmation (called Chrismation) and the Eucharist, while in the Roman rite the same initiation continues through the years of catechesis, to be completed later by Confirmation and the first Eucharist. This difference in discipline does not affect the validity or the dignity of the sacraments: it merely expresses two legitimate and ancient ways of organizing the same Christian initiation.

According to number 1292 of the Catechism, the Eastern practice emphasizes more strongly the unity of Christian initiation, joining in a single liturgical moment birth into the life of grace, the gift of the Holy Spirit, and full participation in the Eucharist. For this reason, in the East, it is common for the same priest who baptizes to also administer Chrismation — something that, in the Latin discipline, is normally reserved to the bishop — always using the "myron" (chrism) previously consecrated by a bishop.

This unity has a practical and theological reason: it allows the Eastern Christian to receive Holy Communion from infancy, joining the three sacraments of initiation in a single celebration and avoiding the long interval of years that, in the West, now separates Baptism from Confirmation.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1233, 1292

itens.titulo: The Indelible Sacramental Character
itens.resumo: Baptism, Confirmation, and Holy Orders imprint on the soul a permanent spiritual "seal," which is why none of the three can be repeated.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism teaches, in number 1121, that the sacraments of Baptism, Confirmation, and Holy Orders confer, in addition to grace, a sacramental character or "seal" by which the Christian shares in Christ's priesthood and is part of the Church according to different states and functions. This configuration to Christ and to the Church, brought about by the Holy Spirit, is indelible: it remains forever in the Christian, even if he falls away from the faith or sins gravely.

The character is not merely a passive mark: according to the same number of the Catechism, it is a positive disposition for grace, a promise and guarantee of divine protection, and a vocation to divine worship and to the service of the Church. For this reason, these three sacraments — unlike the Eucharist, Penance, the Anointing of the Sick, and Matrimony — can never be repeated: one who has already been validly baptized, confirmed, or ordained cannot receive them again.

For the confirmand, understanding the indelible character of Confirmation helps to realize that the gift received is neither fleeting nor dependent on momentary religious feelings: it is a definitive mark of the Holy Spirit, who continues to act in the Christian's life even in periods of greater distance or difficulty in faith.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 1121

itens.titulo: The Common Priesthood of the Faithful
itens.resumo: Through Baptism and Confirmation, every Christian shares in the priesthood of Christ and is called to offer his or her life as spiritual worship to God.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism teaches, in number 1268, that the baptized have become "living stones" to be "built into a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood" (cf. 1 Pet 2:5, 9), thus sharing in the priesthood of Christ, in his prophetic and royal mission. This participation is called the "common priesthood of the faithful," distinct from the ministerial priesthood received in the sacrament of Holy Orders, but real and proper to every baptized person.

Confirmation deepens this participation: by binding the Christian more firmly to the Church and enriching him or her with a special strength of the Holy Spirit, it makes him or her more capable of exercising the common priesthood in concrete life — in personal and family prayer, in the offering of one's own life and work united to the sacrifice of Christ in the Mass, and in the public witness of faith before the world.

This doctrine, taken up again by the Second Vatican Council in the constitution Lumen Gentium, reminds us that the Christian life is not limited to attending the sacraments: every baptized and confirmed person is called to live his or her daily existence as a spiritual offering pleasing to God, actively sharing in the priestly mission of Christ.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 1268
1 Peter 2:5, 9
Second Vatican Council, Dogmatic Constitution Lumen Gentium, no. 10

itens.titulo: Sins against the Holy Spirit
itens.resumo: The deliberate and definitive refusal to accept God's mercy, which the Catechism calls unforgivable not because of any limit in grace, but because of a closing of the heart.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism, in number 1864, teaches that God's mercy has no limits, but anyone who deliberately refuses to accept it through repentance rejects forgiveness of his own sins and the salvation offered by the Holy Spirit. This hardness of heart, if carried through to the end, can lead to final impenitence and eternal loss — it is this, and not a specific verbal offense, that tradition calls the "sin against the Holy Spirit," based on the words of Jesus in Mk 3:29 and Mt 12:31-32.

Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit therefore does not consist in uttering certain words, but in consciously opposing the action of the Spirit himself, who is the one who works in us the forgiveness of sins through the love of the Father and the Son. Refusing to recognize one's own need for conversion, or despairing of God's mercy, or presuming that one can be saved without conversion, are concrete forms of this resistance to the Spirit.

Understanding this teaching helps the confirmand better appreciate the very gift of the Holy Spirit received in Confirmation: he is precisely the one who makes sincere repentance and openness to forgiveness possible, so that to close oneself to this action is to close oneself to the only source from which salvation can come.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 1864

itens.titulo: The Witness of Faith and Martyrdom
itens.resumo: The strength of the Holy Spirit received in Confirmation enables the Christian to profess the faith publicly, even to the point of martyrdom if necessary.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism teaches, in number 2473, that martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith: it means bearing witness even unto death. The martyr bears witness to Christ, who died and rose, to whom he is united by charity, and he bears witness to the truth of the faith and of Christian doctrine, enduring death through an act of fortitude. The following number, 2474, recalls that the Church has collected with the greatest care the memories of those who went all the way in confessing their faith, gathered in the ancient Acts of the Martyrs.

The Second Vatican Council links this readiness directly to the gift received in Confirmation: by the sacrament, the faithful are more perfectly bound to the Church, are enriched with a special strength of the Holy Spirit, and hence are more strictly obliged to spread and defend the faith, both by word and by deed, as true witnesses of Christ. This strength, carried to the extreme, is the same that sustained the long line of Christian martyrs who, from the first centuries until today, have not feared to sacrifice their earthly life out of love for Jesus Christ.

In Confirmation catechesis, the theme of martyrdom is not presented as something distant or rare, but as the ultimate horizon of a witness that begins in much simpler, everyday actions: owning one's faith before classmates, defending the truth when it is unpopular, and not being ashamed to pray or to live according to the Gospel.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 2473-2474
Second Vatican Council, Dogmatic Constitution Lumen Gentium, no. 11

itens.titulo: The Choice of a Confirmation Name
itens.resumo: A custom, now optional, in which the confirmand adopts the name of a saint or a biblical figure as a personal patron at Confirmation.
itens.corpo:
In many communities, it is customary for the candidate for Confirmation to choose, in addition to his or her own Baptismal name, the name of a saint or a biblical figure whom he or she admires and wishes to take as a patron and model of Christian life. The practice seeks to express the confirmand's desire to imitate that person's dedication to God, making the day of Confirmation also an occasion to deepen knowledge of the life of a specific saint.

Other confirmands prefer not to adopt a new name and to keep only the name received at Baptism, precisely to underline the close bond between the two sacraments: Confirmation does not begin something new and independent, but brings to fullness the grace already received at Baptism. Both options are legitimate, and the choice (or not) of a Confirmation name is today governed by the guidelines of each diocese or parish, without being a doctrinal requirement of the sacrament itself.

Whichever option is chosen, reflection on personal patron saints, often made already at Baptism, at Confirmation, or at another moment of personal conversion, helps Christians realize that the communion of saints is not an abstract idea: they are concrete persons, with a real life story, whom the Church proposes as companionship and intercession on the journey of each of the faithful.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 2156-2159 (the Christian name)

itens.titulo: The Precepts of the Church
itens.resumo: Five positive and elementary laws, distinct from the Ten Commandments, that guarantee the faithful the indispensable minimum of liturgical and moral life.
itens.corpo:
Besides the Ten Commandments, which express the natural moral law revealed by God, the Catechism presents, in nos. 2041 to 2043, the so-called "precepts of the Church": positive laws established by the pastoral authority to guarantee the faithful the indispensable minimum in the spirit of prayer, moral effort, and growth in the love of God and neighbor. They are usually enumerated as five: to participate fully in Mass on Sundays and holy days of obligation, refraining from unnecessary work; to confess at least once a year; to receive Communion at least during the Easter season; to observe the days of fasting and abstinence established by the Church; and to help provide for the material needs of the Church.

Unlike the Commandments, which apply to every person at every time and place because they flow from human nature itself, the precepts of the Church are ecclesiastical laws, which the competent authority may in principle adjust, adapt, or dispense according to circumstances — although their observance is, for the Catholic, a true obligation of conscience.

The Catechism situates these precepts within a line of moral life linked to the liturgical life and nourished by it: they are not a set of arbitrary rules, but the concrete minimum floor that helps Christians keep their faith from being reduced to a vague feeling, guaranteeing them a regular and visible practice of the sacramental and communal life.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 2041-2043

itens.titulo: The Renewal of Baptismal Promises
itens.resumo: Before the anointing with chrism, the candidate publicly renews the promises of Baptism, professing the faith that he or she is about to receive with renewed strength.
itens.corpo:
In the rite of Confirmation, when celebrated separately from Baptism, the anointing with holy chrism is preceded by the renewal of baptismal promises and the profession of faith by those who are to be confirmed: the bishop (or the priest presiding) asks whether they renounce sin and Satan, and whether they believe in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, following the same structure of questions and answers used at Baptism and at the Easter Vigil.

After this public profession of faith, the bishop extends his hands over all those who are to be confirmed, saying a prayer of strong epicletic content—that is, of invocation and supplication of the Holy Spirit—before performing the properly sacramental act: the anointing with chrism on the forehead of each one, with the laying on of the hand, accompanied by the words "Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit."

By placing the renewal of baptismal promises immediately before the anointing, the liturgy of Confirmation makes visible what theology already teaches: Confirmation is not a sacrament independent of Baptism, but the development and strengthening of a faith that had already been professed—by the parents and godparents, in the case of children—on the day the Christian was baptized.
fontes: Rite of Confirmation (Ordo Confirmationis)
Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 1298

itens.titulo: Oil in Sacred Scripture
itens.resumo: Before becoming the matter of Confirmation, oil was already, in the Old Testament, a sign of the anointing of kings, priests, and prophets by the Spirit of God.
itens.corpo:
In the Old Testament, anointing with oil was the gesture that consecrated someone — or something — to a special mission from God. Kings such as Saul and David were anointed by prophets in the name of the Lord (cf. 1 Sam 10:1; 16:13), priests were consecrated with oil for the service of worship, and the very Hebrew term "mashach" (to anoint) gave rise to the word "mashiach", that is, "anointed one", "Messiah" — the title that the Jews applied to the expected liberator and that Christians recognize as fully fulfilled in Jesus Christ.

The oil used in these anointings was not just any product: Scripture describes a sacred oil, made of olive oil and spices such as myrrh, cinnamon, and cassia, reserved exclusively for liturgical use and for the consecration of persons and objects of worship (cf. Ex 30:22-33), in a clear distinction between what is sacred and what is for common use. Symbolically, oil came to signify the strength and joy of the Spirit of God poured out upon the one anointed.

It is against this biblical background that we understand why the Church chose oil in particular — holy chrism — as the matter of Confirmation: just as kings, priests, and prophets were anointed for a mission, the person to be confirmed is anointed to share more fully in the royal, priestly, and prophetic mission of Christ, strengthened by the same Holy Spirit whom the anointed ones of the Old Testament prefigured.
fontes: Exodus 30:22-33
Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 436, 1289

itens.titulo: The Christian Initiation of Adults
itens.resumo: Unbaptized adults receive Baptism, Confirmation, and the Eucharist in a single celebration, usually at the Easter Vigil, at the end of a catechumenal journey.
itens.corpo:
For adults who come to the Catholic faith without having been baptized, the Church provides a journey of its own, governed by the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults (RCIA), promulgated in 1972 as a fruit of the liturgical reform of the Second Vatican Council. The journey is organized into four periods — pre-catechumenate, catechumenate, purification and enlightenment, and mystagogy — and three rites of passage: the entrance into the catechumenate, the election (or enrollment of names), and, finally, the celebration of the three sacraments of initiation.

Unlike the usual journey in the Latin Church for those baptized as infants — in which Baptism, Confirmation, and the Eucharist are separated by years of catechesis — the adult who comes to the faith already mature receives the three sacraments in a single celebration, normally at the Easter Vigil: first Baptism, immediately followed by Confirmation, and finally the first Eucharist, which completes initiation.

This practice, closer to the unity preserved in the Eastern Churches, shows that the separation between Baptism and Confirmation, common in the West for those baptized as children, is not an essential requirement of the sacrament, but a pastoral discipline that the Church herself can arrange differently according to the concrete situation of those who receive the sacraments.
fontes: Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults (1972)
Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 1233, 1247-1249

itens.titulo: The Lay Apostolate and the Gifts of the Spirit
itens.resumo: The Second Vatican Council teaches, in the decree Apostolicam Actuositatem, that every layperson is called to the apostolate by the very Christian vocation received in Baptism and Confirmation.
itens.corpo:
On November 18, 1965, the Second Vatican Council promulgated the decree Apostolicam Actuositatem on the apostolate of the laity, teaching that this task springs from the Christian vocation itself and therefore can never be lacking in the Church. The document explains that lay people can carry out their apostolic activity either individually or gathered in communities and movements, but that the personal apostolate, the fruit of an authentic Christian life, is the origin and condition of every lay apostolate — including the organized apostolate — and nothing can replace it.

This call is directly linked to the gift received in Confirmation: while Baptism already incorporates the Christian into the mission of the Church, Chrism "binds them more perfectly to the Church" and gives them "special strength" to live this vocation more consciously and courageously, according to each person's own gifts — not only within the walls of the church, but in the workplace, family, study and social life where each layperson is placed.

The decree also recalls that the lay apostolate, although the fruit of each Christian's free initiative, must be exercised in harmony with the pastors of the Church: Confirmation does not make the confirmand independent of ecclesial communion, but enables them to collaborate, with the freedom and responsibility proper to the laity, in the one evangelizing mission entrusted by Christ to the whole Church.
fontes: Second Vatican Council, Decree Apostolicam Actuositatem (November 18, 1965)
Catechism of the Catholic Church, nos. 900-913
